facts.text: Tolleson was founded in 1912 by Walter G. Tolleson, who reopened the Ten Mile Store, the first stagecoach stop on the route to Yuma.
In 1913, Walter's brother Leon became the first postmaster, and the town’s mail route began out of the general store before a dedicated post office was built.
By the 1950s Tolleson earned the nickname “Vegetable Center of the World” thanks to its booming agriculture before mechanization reduced labor needs in the 1960s.
The city’s strategic location—traversed by Interstate 10, Union Pacific Railroad, and State Route 85—made it a hub that attracted major companies like PepsiCo, Bose, and Nabisco.
During the late 1970s, Tolleson expanded from one to six square miles amid a regional “range war” where neighboring cities annexed land around the planned I‑10 corridor.
In the 1980s, distribution centers for Fry’s Food and Drug and Albertson’s opened, sparking industrial growth that positioned Tolleson as a key logistics node between Phoenix and California.
